h1:
Kamphaeng Phet to Nakhon Sawan
A Road Trip Across Lower Northern Thailand
intro: Kamphaeng Phet and Nakhon Sawan sit only about 120 km apart, and Highway 1 connects them in roughly an hour and a half, which makes them a natural pair to string together into an easy driving trip. The Kamphaeng Phet side gives you a World Heritage city and the Western Forest; the Nakhon Sawan side gives you Thailand's largest freshwater lake and the source of the Chao Phraya River. We've laid it out as a 3-day, 2-night plan running north to south, with a day-by-day timeline so you can see exactly what to do each day and where to stop and eat.

blocks.html: This route works best if you have your own car or a rental, since several of the sights are spread out beyond the towns and public transport doesn't reach them easily. The main route itself is very simple: Highway 1 (Phahonyothin) runs straight from Kamphaeng Phet down to Nakhon Sawan. The drive is flat, through plains and rice fields, easy going, with petrol stations and roadside coffee shops at intervals. If you'd rather take a longer way with extra stops, you can detour through Phichit, but the main plan below keeps to the straight line so it's easy to follow.

blocks.text: Route overview and how the days break down

blocks.html: The idea behind the plan is to start in Kamphaeng Phet, since its highlights are the old city and the nature to the west. Once you've covered those, you move down to Nakhon Sawan, the larger city with more places to stay and eat, which makes it a good final stop. The driving legs between points aren't long. The most tiring day is the first, when you head out to Khlong Lan; the rest are relaxed.

items: Day 1 — The Kamphaeng Phet World Heritage city in the morning, then out to the Khlong Lan nature area in the afternoon, overnight in Kamphaeng Phet town.
Day 2 — The temples outside the old city walls in the morning, drive down to Nakhon Sawan around midday, walk Pak Nam Pho in the afternoon and evening, overnight in Nakhon Sawan.
Day 3 — Bueng Boraphet at dawn, a stop at Pasan at the source of the Chao Phraya before heading home.

blocks.title: Rough distances
blocks.html: Kamphaeng Phet to Nakhon Sawan is about 120 km on Highway 1, around an hour and a half. Kamphaeng Phet town to Khlong Lan Waterfall is about 60 km, so budget half a day for the round trip.

blocks.text: Day 1 — World Heritage city + Khlong Lan nature

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: The old city of Kamphaeng Phet, then out to the forest in the west

items.activity: Start at Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park, the zone inside the city walls, and walk Wat Phra Kaeo right beside the palace grounds.
items.note: Go early before the sun gets harsh; it's an easy walk for photos. Entry to the inner-walls zone is a few tens of THB per person.

items.activity: Move on to Wat Phra That in the same zone to see the bell-shaped chedi and the cluster of old stupa bases.
items.note: The park is a World Heritage Site along with Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai, and it's shadier under big trees than many people expect.

items.activity: Lunch in town — try the chicken noodle soup or other Kamphaeng Phet local dishes.
items.note: Chicken noodle soup is the province's signature dish, with old established shops scattered around town.

items.activity: Drive out toward Khlong Lan district, aiming for Khlong Lan Waterfall inside Khlong Lan National Park.
items.note: It's about 60 km from town; the last stretch is a forest road, so take the bends carefully.

items.activity: Walk to Khlong Lan Waterfall, a single large tier with a pool you can swim in during the rainy season.
items.note: In the rainy season (Jun–Oct) the water is full and beautiful; in the dry season there's less, but you can still walk and visit.

items.activity: Drive back into Kamphaeng Phet town, check in, and rest.
items.note: Leave time before dark on the way back, since the forest road has few lights.

items.activity: Dinner along the Ping River or at an evening market in town.
items.note: The riverside spots have relaxed places to sit and catch the cool breeze.

blocks.title: If you'd rather not go far
blocks.html: If driving into the Khlong Lan forest isn't convenient, swap it for a deeper walk through the old city, or visit the Kamphaeng Phet National Museum in town instead. The trip still feels full.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Temples outside town, then down to Nakhon Sawan

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Cover the Aranyik temple group, then drive down to Pak Nam Pho

items.activity: Cover the temples north of the old city walls (the Aranyik zone), starting at Wat Chang Rop, a chedi with stucco elephants around its base.
items.note: The morning light is good, there are fewer people, and it's an easy walk through open forest.

items.activity: Continue to Wat Phra Si Iriyabot to see the large standing Buddha image, of which clear traces still remain.
items.note: The Aranyik temples are close together, just a few minutes' drive apart.

items.activity: Head back into town and pick up egg bananas (kluai khai) and banana products as gifts.
items.note: Kamphaeng Phet egg bananas are sweet, fragrant and thin-skinned, the province's signature take-home gift.

items.activity: Set off for Nakhon Sawan on Highway 1, stopping for lunch roadside or at a petrol-station coffee shop.
items.note: It's a straight, easy drive, about an hour and a half.

items.activity: Arrive in Nakhon Sawan and check in around the Pak Nam Pho area.
items.note: Pak Nam Pho is the city center, with plenty of places to stay and eat and easy to walk around.

items.activity: Walk the old Pak Nam Pho quarter to see the old buildings and the Chinese-community atmosphere.
items.note: Nakhon Sawan has deep Chinese-community roots, clear in its shrines and food.

items.activity: Dinner at the riverside market or a well-known fish-ball noodle shop.
items.note: Pak Nam Pho is known for clown-knifefish ball noodles and riverside food in the evening.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Bueng Boraphet + the source of the Chao Phraya

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Thailand's largest lake, ending at Pasan

items.activity: Head to Bueng Boraphet early, the country's largest freshwater lake, where birds come out to feed in the early morning.
items.note: Winter (Nov–Feb) is migratory-bird season and the best time for birdwatching.

items.activity: Take a boat out to see the lake and the flocks of water birds; you can arrange a boat at the pier on the lakeshore.
items.note: Boat fares are charged per boat or per person depending on the spot, so ask the price before you get on.

items.activity: Visit the Bueng Boraphet aquarium and walk the fish tunnel, which runs more than 20 meters.
items.note: Open roughly 09:00–17:00, with over a hundred freshwater fish species to see; good with kids.

items.activity: Lunch in Nakhon Sawan town before wrapping up the trip.
items.note: Try the Pak Nam Pho-style rice soup with toppings or congee.

items.activity: Stop at Pasan, the landmark at the source of the Chao Phraya, where the Ping, Wang, Yom and Nan rivers meet.
items.note: The riverside architecture makes for good photos; it sits at the Ko Yom headland in Pak Nam Pho.

items.activity: Pick up Nakhon Sawan souvenirs, then head home.
items.note: If you're looping back to Bangkok, take Highway 32 south from here.

blocks.text: Where to base yourself for the nights

blocks.html: This plan has two nights. We suggest the first night in Kamphaeng Phet town so it's easy to head out to Khlong Lan and catch the temples in the morning. For the second night, stay in Nakhon Sawan around Pak Nam Pho, the larger city with a wider range of hotels and food, and close to Bueng Boraphet where you'll go first thing the next morning.

items.name: Stay in Kamphaeng Phet town (Night 1)
items.blurb: Near the Historical Park and the Ping River, easy for heading out to Khlong Lan and catching the temples in the morning.

items.name: Stay in Pak Nam Pho, Nakhon Sawan (Night 2)
items.blurb: Right in the city center with plenty of restaurants, close to Bueng Boraphet and Pasan.

blocks.text: Food not to miss along the way

items.name: Kamphaeng Phet chicken noodle soup
items.blurb: The province's signature dish that locals actually eat, with a well-rounded chicken broth and tender chicken. Old established shops are scattered around town; good for breakfast or lunch before heading out.

items.name: Kamphaeng Phet egg bananas
items.blurb: The province's famous fruit, small, sweet and fragrant with thin skins. Eat them fresh, grilled, or buy them processed as a gift to take home.

items.name: Pak Nam Pho clown-knifefish ball noodles
items.blurb: A Nakhon Sawan highlight, with bouncy fresh-made clown-knifefish balls. The well-known shops in the Pak Nam Pho quarter have been open for decades, and some also serve fish cakes and fried snacks.

items.name: Pak Nam Pho congee and rice soup
items.blurb: Pak Nam Pho is a Chinese-community quarter, and breakfast staples like minced-pork congee and rice soup with toppings are everywhere. Great for breakfast before heading to Bueng Boraphet.

items.name: Nakhon Sawan 100-Year Riverside Market
items.blurb: Evening and night food, with stalls lined up along the river, from rice dishes and rat na to fried oysters and desserts, all easy on the wallet.

items.name: Bueng Boraphet freshwater fish
items.blurb: Around the lake there are restaurants serving freshwater fish straight from local waters. Try grilled fish or fish tom yum for a local meal that suits the setting.

blocks.text: Tips to make the trip smoother

items: Bird season at Bueng Boraphet — Nov–Feb is migratory-bird season; come at dawn for the best shots.
Khlong Lan Waterfall is best in the rainy season — Jun–Oct has the most water, but you can still visit in the dry season.
Start early — both Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park and Bueng Boraphet are cooler and less crowded in the morning.
Fill up before the forest — petrol stations are sparse on the Khlong Lan road, so it's safer to fill up in town first.

faq.q: How far is Kamphaeng Phet from Nakhon Sawan, and how long is the drive?
faq.a: It's about 120 km on Highway 1, around an hour and a half. The route is straight and easy to drive, with petrol stations and roadside coffee shops along the way.

faq.q: How many days do I need for this trip?
faq.a: This plan is laid out as 3 days and 2 nights, which is a good fit. You get the Kamphaeng Phet World Heritage city, the Khlong Lan nature area, and the Bueng Boraphet and Pak Nam Pho side of Nakhon Sawan. If you're short on time, drop Khlong Lan and squeeze it into 2 days.

faq.q: Can I do this route without a car?
faq.a: You can, but it's not very convenient, since sights like Khlong Lan and Bueng Boraphet are outside town and hard to reach by public transport. Renting a car or having your own is far more flexible.

faq.q: What's the best time of year for this route?
faq.a: Winter (Nov–Feb) has good weather and is migratory-bird season at Bueng Boraphet, while Khlong Lan Waterfall is at its best in the rainy season (Jun–Oct). If you want a bit of both, late rainy season into early winter is the sweet spot.

faq.q: What is Pasan in Nakhon Sawan?
faq.a: Pasan is a piece of riverside architecture at the Ko Yom headland in Pak Nam Pho. It marks the source of the Chao Phraya River, where the Ping, Wang, Yom and Nan rivers flow together, and it's a popular spot in the city for photos and relaxing.
